procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 23.09.2022 passed by the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Criminal Appeal Nos. 1215/2022 and 1216/2022.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused filed appeals in the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad (Criminal Appeal Nos. 1215/2022 and 1216/2022) challenging the Trial Court's rejection of their application for statutory bail (default bail) under Section 167(2) of the Cr.PC. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed these appeals.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The original accused, feeling aggrieved by the High Court's dismissal of their appeals, preferred the present appeals (Criminal Appeal Nos. 1045-1046 of 2023) before the Supreme Court, seeking release on statutory bail (default bail) under Section 167(2) of the Cr.PC. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether an accused is entitled to statutory/default bail under Section 167(2) of the Cr.PC on the ground that they were not physically present when the investigating agency's request for an extension of time to complete the investigation was granted?

facts: The accused was arrested on January 29, 2022, and the initial 90-day period for investigation was set to expire on April 29, 2022.
On April 22, 2022, before the 90-day period ended, the investigating agency requested an extension of time to complete the investigation.
The Trial Court granted a 30-day extension on the same day, but the accused was not physically present during this hearing.
The accused was informed of this extension the following day, on April 23, 2022.
On May 10, 2022, the accused filed an application for statutory/default bail, arguing that the first extension was illegal due to their absence, and thus the 90-day period had expired.
A second extension was granted on May 22, 2022, this time in the presence of the accused.
The accused never challenged the legality of either the first or the second extension orders directly.
The chargesheet was ultimately filed within the extended period.
law: The Supreme Court referred to its previous judgments, particularly in the cases of 'Sanjay Dutt' and 'Jigar'.

The established legal principle is that when an investigating agency requests an extension of the investigation period under Section 167(2) of the Cr.PC, the accused must be given notice or be physically present before the court.
The purpose of this requirement is to ensure that the accused has knowledge that an extension is being sought and has been granted.

The Court clarified that while an earlier case ('Hitendra Vishnu Thakur') suggested a formal notice was needed for the accused to oppose the extension, the later Constitution Bench decision in 'Sanjay Dutt' held that the physical presence of the accused is sufficient to meet the requirement.
application: The Court acknowledged the procedural lapse: the accused was not present when the first extension was granted on April 22, 2022.
However, the Court found that the core purpose of the law—ensuring the accused's knowledge—was fulfilled because the accused was informed of the extension the very next day.
Crucially, the accused did not challenge the validity of this first extension order after being informed. Instead, they waited until May 10, 2022, to apply for default bail.

The Court reasoned that at the time the default bail application was made, a valid court order extending the investigation period was already in effect. Therefore, the indefeasible right to default bail had not accrued.
Furthermore, a second extension was later granted in the presence of the accused, which was also not challenged, reinforcing the fact that the investigation period was lawfully extended.
The Court concluded that because the chargesheet was filed within the legally extended timeframe, the claim for default bail was not sustainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the accused's claim for statutory/default bail. It held that despite the initial procedural error of the accused not being present, the underlying legal requirement of ensuring the accused's knowledge was met, the accused failed to challenge the extension order, and a valid extension was in place when the bail application was filed, meaning no right to default bail had arisen.

issue.issue_text: Whether an extension of the period of investigation with retrospective effect is permissible after the initial extension order has been set aside?

facts: In the case before the court, an order extending the time for investigation was already in existence (granted on 22.04.2022 and valid until 22.05.2022) when the accused applied for default bail on 10.05.2022.
Crucially, this extension order had never been challenged or set aside by a higher court.
The accused was aware of this extension but did not mention it in their bail application.
law: The Court referred to the precedent set in *Sayed Mohd. Ahmed Kazmi Vs. State*, which holds that an extension of the investigation period with retrospective effect is not permissible.

However, the Court clarified that this rule applies specifically in situations where an initial extension order has been challenged and set aside, and a fresh extension is sought after the original statutory period has already expired.
application: The Court distinguished the facts of the current case from those in the *Kazmi* case.
The key distinction was that the initial extension order in this case was never set aside; it was valid and in force when the accused sought bail.
Since the original extension was legally valid, the question of granting a *new* extension with retrospective effect did not arise.
The investigation period had been lawfully extended before the accused's right to default bail could mature.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, explaining that the principle against retrospective extensions from the *Kazmi* case is not applicable here. This is because the initial extension order was never set aside and was still in effect, meaning there was no need to consider a retrospective extension. The existing, valid extension prevented the accused's right to default bail from arising.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an accused is entitled to statutory/default bail under Section 167(2) of the Cr.PC on the ground that they were not physically present when the investigating agency's request for an extension of time to complete the investigation was granted?
appellant_arguments: The appellant, relying on the decisions in Hitendra Vishnu Thakur, Sanjay Dutt, Sayed Mohd. Ahmed Kazmi, and Jigar, argued for their right to be released on statutory bail.
respondent_arguments: At the time the accused applied for statutory/default bail (10.05.2022), there was already a valid extension of time for investigation granted by the Trial Court (22.04.2022).
The accused had not challenged this extension order, which had been communicated to them.
Therefore, the application for default bail was not maintainable as it was made during the valid extension period.
The accused did not disclose in their bail application that an extension had already been granted.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an extension of the period of investigation with retrospective effect is permissible after the initial extension order has been set aside?
appellant_arguments: Citing the precedent in Sayed Mohd. Ahmed Kazmi Vs. State, the appellant argued that an extension of the investigation period with retrospective effect is not permissible after the initial order has been set aside.
respondent_arguments: The decision in Sayed Mohd. Ahmed Kazmi is not applicable to the facts of the present case.
In the Kazmi case, the extension was challenged and held to be bad in law, which distinguishes it from the current case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An accused is not entitled to the relief of statutory or default bail when the specific facts and circumstances of the case warrant its denial.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, where two extensions for investigation were granted by the Court and were not challenged, and at the time the default bail application was made there was already a valid extension in place, the accused is not entitled to be released on statutory/default bail, especially when the chargesheet was ultimately filed within the extended period.
legal_tests_applied: The right to default bail is only available after the rejection of an application for extension of the investigation period or when the chargesheet is not filed within the prescribed or validly extended time. (Distinguishing Rambeer Shokeen Vs. State)
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's application for default bail on 10.05.2022 was not maintainable because there was already an existing, unchallenged court order extending the time for investigation.
The appellant failed to challenge the extension orders granted by the court, including a second extension that was granted in the presence of the accused.
The chargesheet was filed within the period of extension, which extinguishes the right to statutory/default bail.

The precedents relied upon by the appellant, such as Rambeer Shokeen, were found to be not applicable to the facts of the case, as in that case, the extension application was still pending when the bail application was made, whereas here, the extension had already been granted.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's argument that at the time the accused applied for statutory/default bail, a valid extension of time for investigation was already in effect.
The court's decision was based on the fact that the chargesheet was filed within the validly extended period, thereby negating the accused's claim to default bail.
The court agreed with the ultimate conclusion reached by the High Court in denying statutory/default bail to the accused based on the specific facts of the case.
